title: Asteroid 44 Nysa Revealed as Solar System's First Three-Lobed World
excerpt: High-resolution imaging from two of the world's most powerful telescopes shows the 75-kilometre asteroid has three distinct lobes and a previously unknown moon.
body:
• Astronomers have identified asteroid 44 Nysa as the first known three-lobed body in the solar system, using the Large Binocular Telescope in Arizona and the Very Large Telescope in Chile.
  • Two deep valleys wrap around Nysa's circumference, connecting three separate lobes through narrow necks in a structure scientists call a "contact trinary."
  • A previously unknown moon roughly one kilometre wide was also discovered orbiting the asteroid at a distance of about 170 kilometres.
  • The findings could offer insight into ancient collisions during the early solar system and the formation of enstatite-rich bodies that share chemical traits with Earth.

Asteroid 44 Nysa, a space rock first spotted in 1857, has turned out to be one of the strangest objects ever observed in the solar system. New high-resolution images reveal it has three distinct lobes connected by narrow necks — the first such structure ever confirmed on an asteroid — along with a tiny, previously unknown moon.

The findings, published in a paper titled Unmasking (44) Nysa: Evidence for a Trilobate Structure, are based on observations from the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) in Arizona and the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile.

A Shape Unlike Any Other

Nysa orbits the Sun in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter and has an average diameter of about 75 kilometres. Astronomers had studied it for over a century, with earlier observations hinting at an elongated or possibly two-lobed shape. But its true form remained unclear until now.

https://x.com/SPACEdotcom/status/2082882239608799392

Using the LBT's SHARK-VIS instrument and the VLT's SPHERE/ZIMPOL camera — both equipped with adaptive optics systems that compensate for atmospheric blurring — a team led by Kate Minker of the Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, captured the highest-resolution images ever taken of the asteroid. The images, combined with a specially constructed three-dimensional model, revealed two prominent valleys wrapping around the asteroid's circumference, creating three separate lobes joined by narrow connectors the team calls "colli."

"The images reveal a remarkably unusual object. The most likely explanation is that Nysa is either a contact trinary, consisting of three connected components, or an extremely irregular coherent body unlike anything we've previously observed."

— Kate Minker, Lowell Observatory

Two-lobed asteroids, known as contact binaries, are relatively common. But a three-lobed structure — a contact trinary — has never been documented before. The discovery places Nysa in a category of its own among the millions of known asteroids.

A Tiny Hidden Moon

The team also detected a previously unknown moon orbiting the asteroid, temporarily designated S/2026 (44) 1. The satellite measures roughly one kilometre in diameter and circles Nysa at a distance of at least 170 kilometres. Its faint light was initially overwhelmed by the asteroid's intense brightness — Nysa is an E-type asteroid, a rare class rich in the iron-free mineral enstatite, which makes its surface highly reflective.

"Our technique is a bit like figuring out Christmas presents while they're wrapped," said Al Conrad, associate staff scientist at the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory and co-author of the study. "You may be wondering whether the box you're eyeing contains a clock radio or a bag of socks, so to get a clue of which it is, you pick it up and get a feel for the weight. In a way, you intuitively are measuring density to find out the composition."

Future observations of the moon's orbit will allow scientists to more precisely calculate Nysa's mass and density, which could help determine what lies beneath the asteroid's unusual surface.

Clues to the Early Solar System

E-type asteroids like Nysa are of particular interest because their enstatite-rich composition suggests they formed close to the Sun and share chemical traits with the building blocks of Earth. Understanding how Nysa got its shape could illuminate processes that took place during the earliest phases of solar system formation, more than four billion years ago.

Scientists have proposed two leading explanations for the trilobate structure. It may have formed through the low-velocity re-accumulation of fragments after an ancient collision, with three pieces — each 20 to 60 kilometres wide — gently merging over time. Alternatively, Nysa could be the remnant of a dramatic hit-and-run collision involving a larger parent body that left it severely deformed but intact.

"These new images appear consistent with several earlier clues that Nysa is not a conventional asteroid," Conrad said. "For the first time, we can directly investigate whether those clues point to a deeply indented body or to a true multi-lobed structure."

What Comes Next

The asteroid's name, fittingly, comes from the mythical land where nymphs raised the Greek god Dionysus — a figure associated with masks and theatre. "In this paper, we're finally unmasking the asteroid's true nature, long after it was discovered," Conrad noted.

If confirmed through additional observations, Nysa would join a growing class of solar system objects whose shapes preserve records of ancient collisions and mergers, offering scientists a window into events that shaped the planets and asteroids we see today. The team plans to use future telescope time to study the moon's orbit in detail and to determine whether Nysa's three-lobed structure is truly a product of separate bodies coming together or the result of a single body being carved apart by impacts.
